title: My Grandmother Lived Alone For Forty Years And Never Spoke About Her Younger Days, And After She Passed The Only Thing Left Was Her Heavy Porch Rocking Chair, But When I Tipped It Over And Found The Seat Stitched Shut By Hand, What I Pulled
excerpt: My grandmother lived alone for forty years in a white farmhouse outside Berea, Kentucky, and in all that time she never once spoke about her younger days.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — THE PORCH
My grandmother lived alone for forty years in a white farmhouse outside Berea, Kentucky, and in all that time she never once spoke about her younger days.

If you asked about her childhood, she would tell you about the weather. If you asked how she met my grandfather, she would say, “At a church picnic, and that’s enough about that.” If you asked why Grandpa had left when my mother was in high school, she would stand up and go check on the pie, even if there was no pie.

Her name was Lillian Hayes, though everybody called her Lil. She grew tomatoes and pole beans, kept laying hens until she was eighty-eight, and sat in the same rocking chair on her front porch every single evening from supper until dark.

It was a heavy, handmade chair of dark walnut, with curved arms worn smooth by her hands and a woven cane seat that had been replaced, at some point, with a padded seat covered in faded blue fabric. Nobody knew where it came from. It had always been there.

My name is Joanne Mercer. I am sixty-one years old, a retired postal clerk from Lexington. I was Grandma Lil’s only granddaughter, and every summer of my childhood I sat on the porch steps at her feet while she rocked and hummed old hymns and watched the road like she was waiting for somebody.
I asked her once, when I was about ten, who she was waiting for. She stopped rocking for a moment. Then she said, “Nobody, honey. Just watching the light go.” And she started rocking again.
I believed her for fifty years. I should have known better. My grandmother never did anything without a reason.
PART 2 — THE CHAIR
Grandma Lil died in February at the age of ninety-four. My mother had passed six years before, so it fell to me to empty the farmhouse.

It took me most of the spring. I gave the furniture to cousins and neighbors and the church thrift shop. I boxed up her quilts and her Bible and her recipe cards. I sold the hens’ old coop to a young couple down the road who were starting a farm. By May, the house echoed when I walked through it.
The last thing left was the rocking chair on the front porch.
I had saved it for the end on purpose. I wanted it. I had always wanted it. I planned to put it on my own porch in Lexington, where I could sit in the evenings and feel close to her.
My son-in-law, Mike, came out on a Saturday with his truck to help me haul it home. He grabbed it by the arms to lift it and grunted.
“Good grief, Joanne,” he said. “What’s this thing made of? Lead?”
I tried lifting one side myself. He was right. It was far too heavy. Much heavier than any rocking chair had a right to be, even one made of solid walnut.
We tipped it over onto its back on the porch boards so Mike could look underneath for a broken rocker or a metal brace. That was when I saw it.

Someone had cut open the bottom of the padded seat. A long, straight slit along the underside, almost the whole width of the chair. And someone had sewn it closed again, by hand, with small, tight, even stitches in heavy blue thread.
I knew those stitches. I had watched them go into a hundred quilts.
“That’s Grandma’s work,” I said quietly. “She sewed that shut herself.”
PART 3 — THE SEAM
Mike looked at me. “You want me to open it?”

I took the little pocketknife from my purse, the one my grandfather gave me before he left, the only thing of his I ever owned. I knelt on the porch boards and carefully cut the blue thread, stitch by stitch, the way Grandma taught me to take out a seam without tearing the fabric.
The padding inside was old cotton batting, yellowed and flat. But beneath it, filling the hollow space under the seat, was a bundle wrapped in oilcloth and tied with a faded red ribbon.
I lifted it out. It was heavy. I untied the ribbon with shaking fingers.
Inside were letters. Dozens and dozens of letters, in envelopes gone soft and brown with age, all addressed to Miss Lillian Carter, my grandmother’s maiden name, in the same bold, slanting hand.
Underneath the letters was a small black velvet box. And under the box, a photograph.

The photograph was of a young woman I barely recognized, laughing in a cotton dress beside a tall young man in work clothes, his arm around her waist. They were standing in front of a sawmill. The young woman was my grandmother, perhaps nineteen years old. I had never seen her laugh like that, not once, in my entire life.
Mike crouched down beside me. “Joanne? Are you all right?”

I could not answer. I was holding the photograph and staring at the young man’s face, and all I could think was that my grandmother had spent forty years sitting on top of this, every evening, watching the road.
“Who is he?” Mike asked gently.
I turned the photograph over. On the back, in faded pencil, it said: Lil and Tom. Carter’s Mill. June 1950.
PART 4 — THE LETTERS
I did not drive home that night. I sat at Grandma’s empty kitchen table under the single bulb and read every letter in order.
There were forty-one of them. The first was dated September 1950. The last was dated October 1984.

His name was Thomas Beale. He had worked at my great-grandfather’s sawmill as a young man. He had fallen in love with the mill owner’s daughter, and she with him. The letters made that very clear. They were not fancy letters. Tom had left school at fourteen. But they were tender and funny and full of plans.
Then, in the fourth letter, things changed.

Your daddy told me today I am not good enough for you, Tom wrote. He says a mill hand with no land will never marry a Carter. He fired me this morning and told me to be off the property by Sunday. Lil, I am going west to work the timber in Oregon. I will make something of myself and come back for you. Wait for me. Please wait.
The letters after that came from logging camps in Oregon. Every one ended the same way: Write to me, Lil. Why don’t you write?
I realized, reading them, that she never had. Or that her letters had never reached him.
The postmarks told the rest. The first letters were opened neatly. But for years, none of them seemed to have been touched at all. They had been opened all at once, much later, and smoothed flat.
My great-grandfather, I suspected, had kept them from her.
And when he died, my grandmother found them all, and read them, and sewed them into the chair she sat in every night for the rest of her life.
PART 5 — THE RING
Inside the black velvet box was a simple gold ring with a tiny chip of a diamond. Tucked into the lid was a slip of paper.
Bought this with my first month’s pay in Oregon, it said in Tom’s handwriting. Hoping to put it on your finger someday. If you are married and happy, keep it anyway, and think of me kindly.
That letter was from 1952. By then, my grandmother had already been married to my grandfather for a year.

I understood then why she never spoke about her younger days. She had believed for years that Tom had simply left and forgotten her. She had married another man, a man who was never very kind and who eventually left too. And then, sometime later, she had learned the truth.

I found the date in the family Bible. My great-grandfather died in 1979. Somewhere in his desk, my grandmother must have found the bundle of letters, kept by a stubborn old man who had decided who his daughter would love.
And then she kept writing, it seemed. Because the last letters from Tom, in the early eighties, were answers. Answers to letters she must have sent him.

I sorted them carefully on the kitchen table. In 1981 he wrote that he was a widower now, with a grown son. In 1983 he wrote that he had a small house outside Eugene, Oregon, with a porch facing west.
And in October 1984, he wrote the last letter.

I built you something, Lil. I built two of them, actually. One for me and one for you. I’m sending yours on the freight train. I’ll sit in mine every evening and you sit in yours, and we’ll watch the same sun go down two thousand miles apart. Maybe someday you’ll come sit beside me. The other chair will always be here.
PART 6 — THE SEARCH
I read that letter four times. Then I went out onto the dark porch and put my hand on the rocking chair.

Tom had built it. With his own hands, in Oregon, in 1984, and sent it across the country on a freight train. And my grandmother had sat in it every evening for the next forty years, watching the road and the setting sun.

She never went to him. I do not know why. Perhaps she was afraid. Perhaps she had my mother and me to think about. Perhaps she simply believed it was too late. She was a woman who rarely let herself want things.

When I got home to Lexington, I asked my granddaughter, Kayla, who is good with computers, to help me search. We found Thomas Beale’s obituary within an hour. He had died in 2011, at the age of eighty-two, in Eugene, Oregon. He had been a timber foreman, then the owner of a small lumber company. He was survived by a son, Daniel, and three grandchildren.
